Here are, in no particular order, my beefs with Mac:

1) Too expensive. You're paying a premium price for hardware that is no better than PC hardware. To top it off, Apple's specifications are typically a year behind present day PCs. So you're paying more for old technology.

3) Non standard ways of doing things. I had an SMB share at work, PCs connected to it fine, Linux machines connected to it fine. Macs connected at around 1/3rd the speed of everything else. It was a known bug at the time in Apple's SMB implementation and, at the time, they showed no inclination to fix it.

4) Apple's general attitude of "we know better than you do". Need to wipe and re-load an iPad? Sorry, they won't let you do that. Problem with the new iOS slowing everything down? Hope you jailbroke it and backed it up first otherwise there's no going back.

5) Hardware problems. Mac fanboys like to say you're paying more because the hardware is better. It's not. In fact, every Apple product in recent memory has had one display problem or another, some even resulting in class action lawsuits. You can't say the same thing for Toshiba or Dell or Lenovo.

The flaw in this thinking is that you assume that the rate at which humans are re-releasing CO2 into the atmosphere matches that of the Earth's natural carbon cycle. Plant life/natural processes do not just absorb CO2 and store it, but rather convert into other carbon-based molecules e.g. hydrocarbons in oil. Most data indicates that humans are not "only barely contributing" but rather accelerating it quite rapidly.

This kind of organism-induced drastic climate change isn't brand new either. For example, when Cyanobacteria evolved the ability to perform photosynthesis around 2.5 billion years ago, the atmosphere had almost no oxygen in it. The capability of such bacteria to exploit CO2 as a resource that other organisms weren't led to their proliferation and ultimately drastic spikes in oxygen concentration. Researchers in this field believe that such drastic increases in O2 levels are responsible for the explosions in evolutionary diversity that line up with the changing atmosphere. Obviously, some species that were adapted to an atmosphere that contained no oxygen lost their evolutionary advantage and likely died off at the expense of such cyanobacteria.

In a more abstracted perspective, maybe the sharp increase in CO2 levels that we are now seeing will one day be classified along with these other drastic changes in atmosphere, and life on Earth will adapt. But considering how long evolutionary adaptation takes, it is clear that some species will be lost because of this, and we are indeed in a mass extinction event.

I guess you could say the Earth isn't in danger or being harmed, but what do you mean when you say that? The Earth was once a lifeless molten rock, so our contribution to the elimination of life on Earth is no big deal? Venus has runaway greenhouse gases and look how it turned out?

I feel like there is cause for alarm because as a self-aware technologically advanced society we are capable of both accelerating the Earth's natural cycle as well as limiting our impact on the environment if as a whole we decided to go down that road. 1st - You could definitely out debate the shit out of me on this, and what you're saying is definitely true, but I got time so I'm going to try harder to get my point across. (And yes I know my logic is flawed but this is why I think this way and why others might be skeptical of people talking about climate change).

I and others hear the whole humans are accelerating climate change. The average person is told that in 100 years the temperature will go up 2 degrees. The average Joe will say "so what? That's not bad." Then if you still have their attention you can tell them what will result from that, and they might start to get concerned. Until they ask, "if I and everyone else stopped putting CO2 in the air will it prevent all of this from happening?" And the answer is no, it'll just delay it. And not by all that much. (I don't know exact numbers and I'm not going to look them up. This is only being written to let you understand why I and others might think this way). The Earth would hit that temperature even if humans had never existed, so what if it hits it a little sooner? Yes by hitting it sooner it'll take out some animals, but how much of a difference will it make? If humans had never existed there would be animals going extinct as the Earth comes out of this ice age. Also, where do we draw the line? How slow can we and how slow should we make the warming? How much effort do we put into allowing or helping each plant and animal to adapt? And how many would we loose anyways? Mass extinction sounds bad, and there has and always will be extinctions. So the questions is, where is the line for acceptable extinction?

Earth was once a lifeless rock, but through all the stuff it's been through over the billions of years it has never come close to returning to that, and putting a very small amount of extra CO2 in the air isn't going to change that. I understand exponential temperature changes, but there are so many factors the Earth has that will counteract ending up like Venus (yes I know Neil Degrass Tyson said that, but it was a off handed remark and not a we have to immediately mobilize ever man woman and child to prevent this, type comment).

We are a technologically advance species and we can slow climate change, or at least our role in it. But why? Not as in why do anything, but as in why should we put all this effort into slowing or stopping it when we should be accepting it and preparing for the future? It will end up at that temperature no matter what. There is farm land that is drying up as we speak. We are holding onto that land, we are putting in a ridiculous amount of time, effort and money into saving it. Farmland that we will have to abandon soon anyways whether or not we stop contributing to climate change.

So why not embrace global warming and prepare to live on a slightly warmer planet? This is going to happen, but humans seem to have this attitude of "I don't wanna change" and it's too much of an inconvenience. I don't like change. I want everything to stay the same. And - I don't want to grow different crops. Or, I don't want to accept that I can't grow anything here and, if I want to farm, I'm going to have to move to a more fertile area.

I'm not skeptical of climate change (which was the original topic) I am skeptical of the culture and attitudes towards it. Should there be cause for alarm? Yes, but that has to be directed in the right way. People need to stop saying and believing the half truths. Like - "If we don't stop releasing CO2 into the air the Earth will warm be 2 degrees in 100 years" - Yes this is true, but it's a half truth. If we stop releasing CO2 into the air the Earth will warm 2 degrees in 125 years or 150 or whatever. We should be accepting global warming as an entire species and preparing for a future with it. But instead I feel that there are a lot of people in the climate change community that word things in such a way, and want people to believe that we can prevent or stop climate change. I feel we should be more alarmed at this. Alarmed that we could waste a ridiculous amount of time, money and effort trying to stop change that is going to happen. We as a species have a choice, either a) put 100% of our time, money, and effort to stop contributing to climate change, or b) 100% into preparing for it, or c) something in between. My argument is that it's going to happen so we need to do either b or c with it being either all or most of or time, money, and effort to preparing.

The thing that bothers me is that this is happening and people believe and repeat half truths. The original topic was "Climate change doubters why are you skeptical" - well I'm skeptical of everyone who says we need to stop global warming, or we need to stop driving SUVs. I'm skeptical of everything that comes out of their mouth because I feel like they are only going to speak half truths.
